title: Coverage of capping ligands determining the selectivity of multi-carbon products and morphological evolution of Cu nanocatalysts in electrochemical reduction of CO2
abstract: Identifying the active sites of Cu nanoparticles that convert CO2 to multi-carbon (C2+) materials has remained elusive. It is caused by the reconstruction of Cu nanoparticles during electrochemical CO2 reduction and the unrevealed effect of capping ligands covering the Cu surface. We show that the C2+ selectivity and morphological evolution of Cu nanoparticles largely depend on the density of the capping ligand, tetradecylphosphonate (TDP). Ultraviolet-ozone pre-treatment of Cu nanoparticles reduced the density of TDP. Desorption of the remaining ligands was expedited within 3 h of the CO2 reduction process, and the concurrent aggregation of NPs formed bare Cu clusters. The increased C2+ selectivity of >50% faradaic efficiency revealed that the existing grain boundaries of Cu clusters promoted CO dimerization to produce C2+ materials. Despite similar cluster formation, Cu nanoparticles without ultraviolet-ozone treatment showed poor C2+ selectivity, suggesting that the remaining TDP, half of the original concentration, passivated the grain boundaries. Further the morphological transformation of Cu did not increase C2+ selectivity even after 20 h of the reaction.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text:
The ability to design nanostructures has started a new era in the development of efficient electrocatalysts. Capping ligands can be used to achieve the optimal size, shape, and structure to target specic electrochemical reactions.1–4 However, nanostructure design is not the only factor that determines catalytic sites. Capping ligands that are located at undercoordinated sites signicantly reduce the catalytic activity.5 They can also tune the electronic structure of the catalyst6,7 and interact with intermediates,8,9 both of which modulate catalytic selectivity. In addition, nanocatalysts can migrate and agglomerate during electrochemical reactions, resulting in creation or loss of active sites.10–12 Identifying catalytic sites for long-term reactions has remained elusive.
These nanocatalyst behaviors have oen been observed in the electrochemical carbon dioxide reduction reaction (CO2RR).10,13–16 CO2 gas can be converted into various chemical species aer the formation of CO (eqn (1)). In this multi-

Their aggregation, forming inter-particle boundaries, might serve as the main active sites. However, the fate of these boundaries for long-term catalysis has not been clearly scrutinized. More importantly, most studies neglected the effect of capping ligands. In particular, ligand-containing Cu catalysts were employed with the assumption of their removal through washing processes.16,23,27 Their C2+ selectivity was various and could not be clearly addressed.12,23,25 Here, we show that residual capping ligands are critical in the creation of C2+ catalytic sites and the restructuring process. We utilized 8 nm diameter Cu nanoparticles (NPs) using a tetradecylphosphonate (TDP) capping ligand. Ultraviolet-ozone (UVO) pre-treatment was initiated to remove TDP, and naked Cu NPs were obtained aer 3 h of reaction. By forming Cu clusters and grain boundaries via aggregation of Cu NPs, the C2+ selectivity increased, exceeding 50% faradaic efficiency (FE). These active sites were stable even aer 20 h of CO2RR. Conversely, the morphological evolution of Cu NPs to cuboidal shape occurred in the absence of UVO treatment. Half of the original TDP remained on the Cu catalysts during the CO2RR, resulting in predominant CO production. We decoupled the surfaceroughness effect via UVO treatment and conrmed the pivotal effect of capping ligands on C2+ selectivity.

sections.heading: Results and discussion
sections.text:
We synthesized colloidal Cu NPs using copper acetate and tetradecylphosphonic acid (TDPA), similar to a previous report.28 The as-prepared Cu NPs had a uniform diameter of 8.11 0.52 nm, and the X-ray diffraction (XRD) pattern exhibited
This journal is © The Royal Society of Chemistry 2021
strong signals for metallic Cu (Fig. 1a and S1a–c†). This reects the dense coverage of TDP capping ligands on the Cu NPs. The phosphonate group of TDP is strongly bound to the Cu surface, while the long alkyl chain tail groups are closely packed and passivate the NP surface. We also observed a small cuprous oxide (Cu2O) signal as evidence of partial oxidation by desorption of the TDP ligand. Interestingly, the longer the Cu NPs were stored in hexane, the more TDP ligands were desorbed, resulting in improved C2+ selectivity in the CO2RR (see details in ESI Fig. S1–S4†). To systematically control the density of TDP over the Cu NPs, we attempted UVO treatment (Fig. 1b).29–32 A Cu NP array was deposited on porous carbon substrates using Cu NPs that were synthesized within a week, and UVO irradiation was performed for 1 to 7 h. Pristine Cu NPs and n hour UVO-treated Cu NPs are denoted hereinaer as p-Cu and nUVO-Cu, respectively. Surface analysis of p-Cu using X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) revealed partial oxidation of the Cu surface, indicated by the Cu0/Cu+ signal at 933 eV in the Cu 2p binding energy (BE) region and the O–Cu bond signal at 530 eV in the O 1s BE region (Fig. 1c).33 Aer UVO treatment, an additional signal designated to Cu2+ was observed in the Cu 2p and 3s BE regions.33 The Cu2+ content increased to 80% of the total Cu species aer 5 h of UVO treatment (Table 1). Coincidently, the phosphonate signal at 132.5 eV was attenuated,34 and the P/Cu ratio was reduced to 70% of the original value aer 5 h of UVO treatment (Table 1). Moreover, the carbonyl functionality was pronounced, demonstrated by an increase in the O]C/Cu ratio by more than 4 fold (Fig. 1c and Table 1). Because the blank carbon substrate did not show any profound O]C signals aer UVO treatment (Fig. S5 and S6†), we excluded the possibility of substrate oxidation. Besides, 5UVO-Cu on Au lm exhibited a absorption band corresponding to the n(C]O) in the attenuated total reectance-infrared spectrum,35,36 for which the TDPA precursor, Au substrate, and p-Cu could not be responsible (Fig. S7†).37 Therefore, we attribute the presence of the carbonyl group to oxidation of the alkyl chains of the capping ligands (Fig. 1b). The surfaces of the Cu NPs were found to be hydrophilic, indicating that aggregated 5UVO-Cu NPs were redispersed in hexane (Fig. S8a†).38 On the carbon substrate, however, the Cu NPs preserved the monolayered arrays without any aggregation even aer 5 h of UVO treatment (Fig. S8b†).

The ratio of FEC2H4 to FEC2H5OH remained constant between 2.3–2.5 aer 1.5 h and 3 h of CO2RR, implying a parallel increase of both C2 products (Table S2†). 7UVO-Cu showed a lower FEC2+ of 45% because long UVO irradiation induced the coalescence of Cu NPs (Fig. S9†).39 Product selectivity was potential-dependent, and the maximum C2H4 yield was observed at 0.98 V, forming 29.3% FEC2H4 for 5UVO-Cu (Fig. 2c, S10, S11 and Table S3†). It is noteworthy that the catalytic selectivity is drastically changed for 5UVO-Cu during 3 h of CO2RR. At the initial stage (<30 min), CO selectivity was predominant for all electrodes. However, 5UVO-Cu showed a signicant increase in C2H4 production at the expense of CO over 30 min of the reaction (Fig. 2d and S12†). Similar selectivity crossings in the plots were also observed for other UVO-treated electrodes (Fig. S13†). In sharp contrast, p-Cu maintained a constant FECO of 32.9% and FEC2H4 of 13.0% throughout the 3 h reaction under similar conditions with a constant CO2 ow of 20 sccm (Fig. 2e).
We hypothesized that the enhanced C2+ selectivity of 5UVOCu by UVO treatment was attributed to three possible factors: the carbon substrate, Cu NPs, and the capping ligand. For the carbon substrate, the surface was mildly oxidized to form O–H functional groups (Fig. S6†). This gentle oxidation did not alter the hydrophobicity of the substrates, validated by the comparable contact angles of water droplets on the 5 h UVO-treated and pristine carbon substrates (Fig. S14†). Thus, the coverage of the aqueous medium and dissolved CO2 gas should be similar for all substrates. The next consideration was the oxidation of Cu NPs, comprising 64% and 80% Cu2+ for

Several studies have reported enhanced C2+ selectivity aer electrochemical oxidation22,40 and O2-plasma treatment of Cu catalysts.41,42 Cuenya et al. reported that thick copper oxide was formed on Cu foil via O2-plasma treatment and increased the C2+ production.41,42 While they suggested that the stable Cu+ subsurface underneath the Cu was the origin of C2+ selectivity, more recent studies using various operando tools demonstrated complete reduction of the copper oxides once the CO2RR began.43–46 We also observed the loss of the Cu+ signal of p-Cu in correlation with emerging Cu0 under CO2RR conditions using in situ X-ray absorption near-edge structure (Fig. S15†). A more plausible explanation for the enhanced C2+ selectivity is the reconstruction of the Cu structure through reduction of Cu+/Cu2+. The reduction of the oxide layer during the CO2RR establishes a rough surface, on which many defects and undercoordinated sites are present. Bell et al. treated Cu foil with Ar-plasma and found that the resulting surface roughness was responsible for improved C2+ selectivity.47 Unfortunately, this analytical method is not applicable to our Cu NPs because the effect of surface oxidation cannot be decoupled from that of the capping ligand. As an alternative, we attempted to use ligand-free Cu catalysts, such as electropolished Cu foil and oxide-derived (OD) Cu NPs. The 5UVO-Cu foil exhibited >5 times the electrical double-layer capacitance (EDLC) of the pristine Cu foil (Fig. S16a and Table S4†). The enlarged electrochemical surface area corresponds to 1.4-fold higher root-mean-square roughness (Fig. S17a†). However, there was a negligible increase in C2+ selectivity, showing 36% of FEC2+ for both 5UVO-Cu foil and pristine Cu

The morphological evolution of Cu NPs is another key to understanding the distinct C2+ selectivity. The dissolution of Cu2+ and Cu+ from the as-prepared Cu NPs occurs around the open circuit potential (OCP), while the Cu NPs were stable at 0.98 V without any loss of Cu ion.27,51 Indeed, we detected only <1 wt% of Cu ions aer 3 h of CO2RR (Table S9†), which insignicantly inuenced the shape change of Cu NPs. Other more important behaviors are the migration and agglomeration of the Cu NPs at the given negative potential, which reduce the surface energy of the Cu material.52,53 The aggregated NPs formed clusters aer 1 h of CO2RR, compared to immobile Cu NPs at the OCP (Fig. S23, S24† and 3c). If the capping ligands are entirely desorbed during the CO2RR, these grain boundaries of clusters can serve as C2+ catalytic sites, as is the case for 5UVO-Cu (Scheme 1).14,54 In comparison, while analogous Cu clusters appeared in the p-Cu, the C2+ selectivity was poor, suggesting the presence of passivated grain boundaries with TDP (Fig. 3d and Scheme 1).

When the CO2RR duration was extended to 20 h aer preelectrochemical activation (1 h CO2RR), the shape of the Cu cluster was retained for 5UVO-Cu, and a FEC2H4 of 30% was constant (Fig. 4a and b). This result supports that the grain boundaries are catalytic sites, particularly for yielding C2H4, and stable for 20 h. In contrast, the Cu clusters in the p-Cu coalesced and formed sub-micron polyhedron particles aer 7 h, followed by cuboidal shapes aer 20 h (Fig. 4d and Scheme 1).52,53 The FECO also signicantly diminished in 3–9 h, demonstrating that some C1 catalytic sites were inactivated during this restructuring process (Fig. 4c). The desorption of TDP was negligible aer the 3 h reaction, showing that half of the original value still remained aer 20 h of CO2RR (Fig. S25†). These results suggest that the dramatic morphological change occurs due to the restructuring of idle Cu that does not engage in the catalytic reaction. One may consider the participation of the CO intermediate in the morphological transformation. Presumably, the morphological evolution was continuous aer the CO2RR and through the subsequent airdrying process.10,12 The most signicant features of these Cu catalysts, we suggest, are clusters and polyhedron particles according to different restructuring processes, originating from the coverage of capping ligands and the number of C2+ active sites. We also note that the effect of capping ligands depends on the ligands, metal catalysts, and applied potentials (Table S10†). Thus, the role of organic ligands linked with catalysts would be systematically studied further by developing molecular libraries and surface engineering.

sections.heading: Conclusions
sections.text: In summary, we demonstrated two pivotal behaviors of Cu NPs dependent on the surface coverage of TDP capping ligands. When TDP was partially removed through UVO pre-treatment, fast and almost complete desorption of the residual ligand occurred during 3 h of CO2RR. Concomitantly, aggregated Cu NPs formed bare grain boundaries, serving as stable active sites for producing multi-carbon products for 20 h of CO2RR. In contrast, around half of the TDP ligands were still adsorbed on the Cu nanocatalyst that was not pre-treated with UVO irradiation. Despite the analogous shape of Cu clusters for both samples, the pristine Cu NPs predominantly yielded CO because TDP might passivate the grain boundaries. These clusters were further transformed into polyhedron particles and cubes, but improved neither ethylene nor CO selectivity. This study provides a better understanding of the role of capping ligands and gained insight into the restructuring process for improving the selectivity of high-value chemical compounds.

sections.heading: Chemicals and materials
sections.text:
Trioctylamine (98%), tetradecylphosphonic acid (97%), copper(I) acetate (97%), potassium bicarbonate ($99.95%), phosphoric acid (85 wt% in H2O, 99.99%) and sulfuric acid (95.0– 98.0%) were purchased from Sigma-Aldrich. Chloroform (GR grade), ethyl alcohol (99.5%, anhydrous), and acetone (99.5%) were bought from Daejung Chemicals & Metals. sections.heading: Synthesis of copper nanoparticles
sections.text:
Synthesis of copper nanoparticles (Cu NPs) was carried out as per the previous report.28 Briey, 10 ml of trioctylamine was preheated at 130 C for 30 min under an argon (Ar) atmosphere. Under anaerobic conditions, the temperature was cooled down to r. t., and 1 mmol of copper(I) acetate and 0.5 mmol of tetradecylphosphonic acid (TDPA) were added. Subsequently, the temperature of the solution mixture was rst increased to 180 C at a ramp rate of 5 Cmin 1 under Ar purging and vigorous stirring conditions and continuously increased up to 270 C at 3 C min 1. Aerward, the solution was cooled down to 100 C and isolation was carried out using 10 ml of anhydrous ethanol, and then the solution was centrifuged at 8500 rpm for 15 min. The resulting Cu NPs were washed with a mixture of chloroform/acetone (1/1 volume ratio) 3 times and dispersed in hexane that was degassed by Ar purging for at least 30 min.

sections.heading: Cu NPs
sections.text:
Aer adjusting the concentration of the NP solution to 0.5 mg ml 1, a 5 ml aliquot of the Cu NP solution (a total 100 ml) was drop-cast onto 1 cmgeo
2 of carbon paper (GDL) repeatedly until the ideal mass loading became 50 mg. Complete Cu NP deposited electrodes were dried in air. For UV-ozone (UVO) treatment, the Cu NP-deposited electrodes were irradiated with UV light (l ¼ 253.7 and 185 nm) inside a custom-built metallic container. The distance between the sample and UV lamp was 5 mm. The power of the lamp was 53 mW cm 2. As control electrodes, Cu foil and oxide-derived Cu NPs (OD Cu NPs) were prepared. Cu foil (Alfa Aesar, 99.9999% purity, 0.1 mm thickness) was electrochemically polished in a symmetric Cu cell, where a voltage of 2 V was applied for 300 s in 85% phosphoric acid (H3PO4) solution. The Cu foil was then washed with DI water and stored under vacuum. The OD Cu electrode was made using cyclic voltammetry (CV) in the potential range of 0.3 V to 1.7 V vs. Ag/AgCl and a scan rate of 20 mV s 1 in CO2-saturated 0.1 M KHCO3(aq) containing 32 mM KCl.22 The working electrode (WE) was the electropolished Cu foil, and the counter electrode (CE) and the reference electrode (RE) were Pt foil and Ag/AgCl (sat. KCl), respectively. The nal OD Cu nanocatalyst was mildly washed with DI water and stored under vacuum.

Helium (He) and argon (Ar) gases were used as the carrier gases for the Plot Q column and Molsieve 5A, respectively. Gas products were collected in a sampling loop every 10 min, and directly injected into the GC. Liquid products were quantitatively analyzed using 1H NMR (Agilent DD2 NMR spectroscope, 600 MHZ). Liquid samples were prepared by mixing 540 ml of the electrolyte solution, 30 ml of 10 mM dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) in D2O, and 30 ml of 50 mM phenol in D2O that served as the internal standard. 1H NMR was carried out with 48 scans for each measurement, and the water suppression (solvent presaturation) technique was implemented to reduce the water signal. The faradaic efficiency (FE) of each product was calculated using eqn (4)–(6),

Electrical double-layer capacitance (EDLC) measurements
EDLC measurements were performed to dene the electrochemical active surface area (ECSA) of the electrodes. Cyclic voltammetry (CV) was performed within a potential range of 0.15 V to 0.2 V vs. Ag/AgCl under the same H-cell condition

afore-mentioned. The scan rates (y) of CV ranged from 4 to 32 mV s 1, and the capacitive current density (jc) was calculated at 0.18 V by the difference between cathodic (jcathodic) and anodic current densities (janodic). The resulting jc was plotted as a function of y, where the slope indicates the capacitance of the electrode, as shown in eqn (7):

where A is the current, s is the time, V is the voltage, and Q is the charge.

sections.heading: Characterization
sections.text: A UV-Vis spectrometer (Shimadzu UV-1800) was used to plot the extinction spectrum of the Cu NPs. The morphology of the Cu NPs deposited on GDL was observed using a eld emission scanning electronmicroscope (FE-SEM, FEIMagellan 400 at 5 kV, 50 pA) equipped with an energy-dispersive X-ray spectrometer (EDS), and transmission electron microscope (TEM, FEI Tecnai F30 ST at 300 kV) at the KAIST Analysis Center for Research Advancement (KARA). All TEM samples were prepared by dropcasting 2–3 droplets of diluted Cu NP hexane solution onto carbon-coated copper grids (Electron Microscopy Science, 300 mesh). X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS, Thermo VG Scientic K-alpha) analysis was achieved by using a monochromatized Al Ka source (1486.6 eV). The binding energy of the core levels was calibrated based on the sp2 hybridized carbon (284.5 eV). An X-ray diffractometer (XRD, BRUKER D2 PHASER, Cu Ka radiation) was used to identify the crystallinity of Cu, Cu2O, and CuO. All XRD samples were dried in a vacuum and were contained in silicon (Si). Atomic force microscopy (AFM, Agilent 5500) images of Cu foil were taken in the tapping mode using an Al-coated silicon tip (42 Nm 1 of force constant, 4.0 mm of thickness NCHR type, Nanoworld). Gwyddion soware was used for three-dimensional image generation. Attenuated total reection infrared (ATR-IR) spectroscopy (Nicolet iS50, Thermo Scientic) identied molecular vibration modes of the capping agent covering the Cu NPs. A contact angle analyzer (Phoenix 300 Plus) was used to measure the contact angle of water droplets on carbon substrates. Inductively coupled plasma optical emission spectroscopy (ICP-OES, Agilent ICP5110) was performed to measure dissolved Cu. Calibration was conducted using multielement standard solutions (Calibration mix 2, Agilent) with 5 different concentrations of 0.01, 0.05, 0.1, 0.5, and 1.0 ppm. To prepare the sample solutions, 1 M H2SO4(aq) was added to both an as-prepared electrolyte solution and a tested solution for 3 h CO2RR. The Cu content was measured at three different wavelengths of 213.598 nm, 324.754 nm, and 327.395 nm. In situ X-ray absorption near-edge structure (XANES) analysis was performed in the Pohang Accelerator Laboratory (PAL) 8C beamline. Cu Kedge spectra obtained in the uorescence mode were analyzed using the Athena soware with the IFEFFIT library.
